mainTopic: The extra leap-year month in a rental (רב, שמואל, and רב נחמן), and who must prove that rent was paid on the due date.
overview: The amud opens with the end of a משנה about renting a bathhouse in ציפורי for 'twelve gold coins a year, a gold dinar a month'. In that case, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and רבי יוסי ruled that the two sides split the extra leap-year month. The גמרא asks how this story fits the משנה's earlier rule that a yearly rental gives the extra month to the renter. It answers that the משנה is missing a case (חסורי מחסרא): mixed wording means a split. רב says he would give the whole month to the landlord, because we follow the last words (תפוס לשון אחרון), even when they truly contradict the first words. שמואל explains that the month is split only when they come to court mid-month, since whoever holds the thing in question keeps it, and the גמרא defends him from a grain-sale ruling. רב נחמן gives the month to the landlord because land stays with its owner, even if the wording is reversed. Then a new question is asked of רבי ינאי: if a renter says he paid and the landlord denies it, who must bring proof? The גמרא narrows this to a claim made on the due date itself, and רבי יוחנן begins to show that a משנה already answers it.

steps.title: The story ends: the judges split the leap month
steps.stepSummary: The משנה finishes the ציפורי story: the case came before רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and רבי יוסי, and they ruled that the extra month should be split.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case came before רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and רבי יוסי, and they said: the landlord and renter should split the extra leap-year month.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of the משנה. It tells us how two great rabbis ruled in a real case about a bathhouse rental in a leap year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rental was agreed at 'twelve gold coins a year, a gold dinar a month.' The first half sounds like a yearly rental, where the extra month would be free. The second half sounds like a monthly rental, where the renter would pay for it. Because the words point both ways, the judges split the extra month between the two sides.

keyTerms.meaning: The extra month added in a leap year

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא מַעֲשֶׂה לִפְנֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
phrases.english: And the incident came before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
and before Rabbi Yosei,
and they said: They should divide the extra month.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבָא מַעֲשֶׂה לִפְנֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the rental used both a yearly and a monthly price, the extra leap month is split between landlord and renter.

steps.title: How can a story contradict the rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised: the משנה just ruled that a yearly rental gives the extra month to the renter, yet the story has the judges splitting it.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: Is a story brought to contradict the rule?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a challenge. A story in a משנה should prove the rule it comes after, but this one seems to go against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the משנה said that if you rent 'for a year' and the year gets an extra month, the renter gets that month for free. In the story, the renter also rented 'twelve gold coins a year,' yet the judges did not give him the month for free; they split it. A story is supposed to back up the rule, not break it.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: An incident to contradict?!
phrases.notes: The incident seems to clash with the earlier ruling in the same משנה, that a yearly rental gives the extra month to the renter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the story at the end of the משנה fits the משנה's earlier ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fit between the ציפורי story and the משנה's ruling on yearly rentals
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A story should support the rule before it. Here the rule gives the month to the renter, but the story splits it, so the story seems to contradict the rule.

steps.title: The משנה is missing a case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה leaves out a middle case. If someone says both 'twelve a year' and 'a dinar a month,' they split, and the story proves exactly that case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is missing words, and this is what it teaches: if he said 'twelve gold coins a year, a gold dinar a month,' they split. And there was also a case in ציפורי of someone who rented a bathhouse using those exact words. It came before רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and רבי יוסי, and they said to split the extra month.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the problem by adding a missing case to the משנה. The story is not about a plain yearly rental; it is about this mixed wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are three cases. 'Per year' means the renter gets the month. 'Per month' means the landlord gets paid. Mixed wording means they split. The story now proves the third case instead of contradicting the first. The גמרא repeats the story's words because it is rebuilding the full משנה text.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what it teaches

steps.confusionAlert: The second telling of the story is not a new case. The גמרא repeats it on purpose because it now belongs to the missing 'mixed wording' case.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three cases: 'per year' gives the month to the renter, 'per month' gives it to the landlord, and mixed wording means they split it.

phrases.english: It is missing words
and this is what it teaches:
But if he said to him
for twelve gold coins per year,
a gold dinar per month – they divide.
And there was also an incident in Tzippori
with one who rented a bathhouse from his fellow
for twelve gold coins per year,
a gold dinar per month,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא מַעֲשֶׂה לִפְנֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
phrases.english: and the incident came before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
and before Rabbi Yosei,
and they said: They should divide the extra month.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by adding a missing case to the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rebuilding the text (חסורי מחסרא): adding a missing middle case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story seemed to be about a plain yearly rental, so it looked like it contradicted the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The story is about mixed wording ('per year' and 'per month'). That is a separate case where the month is split.

steps.title: רב would give the whole month to the landlord
steps.stepSummary: רב says that if he had been the judge, he would have made the renter pay for the full extra month.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: If I had been there, I would have given all of it to the landlord.
steps.whatsHappening: רב disagrees with the ruling in the story. He says the landlord should get paid for the whole extra month.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last words of the rental terms were 'a gold dinar per month.' רב goes by those last words, so the deal is a monthly rental. In a monthly rental the renter pays for every month, including the extra one.

keyTerms.meaning: The landlord (the one who rents out)

phrases.english: Rav said: If I had been there,
I would have given all of it to the landlord.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different ruling from the one in the story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the mixed-wording case, the whole extra month goes to the landlord, because the last words were 'per month.'

steps.title: What is רב adding?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב is teaching. Is he just repeating the rule that we follow a person's last words?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? That we 'hold on to the last expression'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions why רב needed to say this. If his reason is simply 'go by the last words,' that rule is already known.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's ruling fits the known rule of תפוס לשון אחרון: when someone says two things that clash, you follow what he said last. If that is all רב means, his statement seems to add nothing new. This sets up the גמרא's next move, which will explain what רב really adds.

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
'Hold on to the last expression'!
phrases.notes: The גמרא is saying that if this rule is all רב means, there was no need for him to say it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רב's statement adds anything new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's ruling seems to rest only on the known rule of תפוס לשון אחרון, so it looks like it teaches nothing new.

steps.title: Proof that רב already taught the last-words rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its question by showing that רב already ruled, in a sale case, that we follow the last amount named.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רב already said this once! As רב הונא reported from בי רב: if a seller says 'an אסתירא, a hundred coins,' the buyer pays a hundred coins. If he says 'a hundred coins, an אסתירא,' the buyer pays an אסתירא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is backing up its question from step 5 by bringing a source where רב already taught that the last words count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the coin case, the buyer always pays whichever amount the seller said second. That is exactly the rule of following the last words. So the question becomes sharper: why would רב need to say it again about the extra month?

keyTerms.meaning: a coin worth a little less than a hundred small coins

phrases.english: But רב already said this one time!
As רב הונא said:
They say in the study hall of רב:
'An אסתירא, one hundred coins': he pays one hundred coins.
phrases.notes: An אסתירא is worth a bit less than a hundred small coins, so the two amounts don't quite match.

phrases.english: 'One hundred coins, an אסתירא': he pays an אסתירא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the question in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That רב's ruling on the extra month seems to repeat something he already taught
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב הונא's report from בי רב about the אסתירא and the hundred coins

steps.title: The coin case could be read as just explaining
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that from the coin case alone, we might think the second phrase was only explaining the first, so רב had to teach the rule for a real clash.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we had it only from there, I would have said the second phrase is just explaining the first. So רב teaches us here that we follow the last words even in a real clash.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: רב's new ruling is not a repeat, because it teaches something the coin case could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אסתירא and a hundred coins are almost the same amount, so the second phrase could just be making the first more exact. 'Twelve a year' and 'a dinar a month' truly disagree when there is an extra month. רב's ruling shows the last words win even in a true contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have said (a mistaken first thought)

steps.whatToRemember: רב follows the last words even when they truly contradict the first words, not only when they just explain them.

phrases.english: If we had it only from there, I would have said:
he is just explaining his first words,
so he teaches us here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in steps 5 and 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases: explaining versus truly contradicting
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the coin case, we might think the last words count only because they explain the first words.
steps.terutzMaskana: The last words count even when they clearly contradict the first words.

steps.title: שמואל: the split depends on when they came to court
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the month is split only when the case came to court in the middle of the month. At the start, the landlord gets it all; at the end, the renter keeps it all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל said: we are dealing with someone who came in the middle of the month. But if he came at the beginning of the month, all of it goes to the landlord. If he came at the end of the month, all of it goes to the renter.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives his own explanation of the ציפורי ruling that split the extra month.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike רב, שמואל treats it as unclear whether the last words win. So whoever is holding on to what's in question keeps it. At the start of the month the landlord still holds the house and can demand rent. At the end the renter holds the money and cannot be forced to pay.

phrases.english: And שמואל said:
We are dealing with one who came in the middle of the month.
phrases.notes: 'Came' means came to court to settle the argument.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בָּא בִּתְחִלַּת חֹדֶשׁ – כּוּלֵּיהּ לְמַשְׂכִּיר,
phrases.english: But if he came at the beginning of the month, all of it goes to the landlord;
if he came at the end of the month, all of it goes to the renter.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: בְּבָא בְּאֶמְצַע חֹדֶשׁ עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different view from רב's on the extra month.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The extra month is split only when they come to court mid-month. At the start of the month it all goes to the landlord, and at the end it all stays with the renter.

steps.title: Doesn't שמואל elsewhere follow the last words?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל from a ruling of רב and שמואל on selling grain, where the last words decide the outcome.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did שמואל really say we don't follow the last words? But רב and שמואל both say: if a seller says 'I am selling you a כור for thirty,' he can back out even at the last סאה. If he says 'a כור for thirty, a סאה for a סלע,' the buyer acquires each סאה as it is handed over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's explanation by showing that he himself ruled to follow the last words in a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'A כור for thirty' makes the whole כור one sale, so nothing is final until it is all delivered. Adding 'a סאה for a סלע' turns it into many small sales, and that last phrase decides. So שמואל seems to follow the last words, which clashes with step 8.

keyTerms.meaning: hold on to the last expression
a large measure, equal to thirty סאה
to back out of the deal
each one is acquired as it comes

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about grain prices. It is about whether שמואל follows the last words, which the grain case suggests he does.

phrases.english: Did שמואל really say
that we do not say 'hold on to the last expression'?
But רב and שמואל both say:
'I am selling you a כור for thirty':
phrases.notes: A כור is thirty סאה, so this works out to a סלע per סאה, but he didn't say so.

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ אֲפִילּוּ בִּסְאָה אַחֲרוֹנָה!
phrases.english: he can back out even at the last סאה!

phrases.aramaic: כּוֹר בִּשְׁלֹשִׁים, סְאָה בְּסֶלַע אֲנִי מוֹכֵר לָךְ –
phrases.english: 'I am selling you a כור for thirty, a סאה for a סלע':
each one is acquired as it is handed over.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל לָא אָמְרִינַן ״תְּפוֹס לָשׁוֹן אַחֲרוֹן״
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view that we are unsure whether to follow the last words
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the grain sale, רב and שמואל let the last phrase ('a סאה for a סלע') decide, which shows שמואל does follow the last words.

steps.title: The grain ruling was about holding, not about last words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge to שמואל. In the grain case, the reason was that the buyer was already holding the grain. In the bathhouse case, each side is holding something too.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, what is the reason? Because he is holding it. Here too, he is holding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 9 by giving a different reason for the grain ruling. The ruling was not about following last words. It was about who was already holding the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that שמואל follows the last words in the grain case. The גמרא says the true reason there is תפיסה: the buyer already holds the grain. In the bathhouse case, each side holds something (the landlord holds the property, the renter holds the money). So the same reasoning explains שמואל's ruling: each side keeps what he holds, depending on when they come to court.

keyTerms.meaning: he is holding / has taken hold

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think שמואל agrees here that last words decide. The גמרא is saying his grain ruling was never based on last words at all. It was based on who holds the item.

phrases.english: There, what is the reason?
phrases.notes: 'There' means the grain sale case from Step 9.

phrases.english: Because he is holding it.
phrases.notes: The buyer had already taken hold of the grain.

phrases.english: Here too, he is holding.
phrases.notes: In the bathhouse case, the landlord holds the property and the renter holds the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 9 against שמואל
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different reason for the source used in the challenge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל's grain ruling shows that he follows the last words.
steps.terutzMaskana: The grain ruling rests on holding (תפיסה), not on last words. In the bathhouse case, the landlord holds the property and the renter holds the money. So whoever holds keeps: at the start of the month the landlord gets paid, at the end the renter keeps his money, and in the middle the month is split.

steps.title: רב נחמן: Land stays with its owner
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן gives his own ruling: land stays in the owner's possession, so the landlord gets the extra month.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן said: Land stays in the presumed possession of its owner.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא, רב נחמן, gives his ruling on the extra leap-year month. He sides with the landlord.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן uses the rule that קרקע בחזקת בעליה. Rented land still counts as belonging to its owner. So when the deal is unclear, the landlord gets the extra month's rent.

keyTerms.meaning: in the presumed possession of its owner

phrases.english: And רב נחמן said:
Land stays in the presumed possession of its owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third view alongside רב and שמואל
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because land remains in its owner's possession, the landlord receives the extra leap-year month.

steps.title: Isn't רב נחמן just saying what רב said?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב נחמן adds. If his point is to follow the last words, that is just רב's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? 'Hold onto the last statement'? That is the same as רב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's ruling as adding nothing new. It sounds like the same result רב already gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the story's wording, 'a gold dinar per month' comes last, so following the last words also gives the landlord the month. If that is all רב נחמן means, he is just repeating רב.

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
'Hold onto the last statement'?
That is the same as רב!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling just given in Step 11
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If his ruling only gives the result of following the last words, it is the same as רב's ruling and adds nothing.

steps.title: Even when the order is reversed, the landlord wins
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן's ruling is different from רב's. The landlord gets the month even when the wording is in the opposite order.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב נחמן goes further than רב. He gives the month to the landlord even when the order of the words is flipped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב decides by which phrase came last. רב נחמן decides by who owns the land. So if the deal ends with 'twelve a year,' רב would side with the renter, but רב נחמן still sides with the landlord.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three views on the extra month. רב follows the last words. שמואל goes by who is holding: the month is split only when they come to court in the middle of the month; at the start the landlord gets it all, and at the end the renter keeps it all. רב נחמן gives it to the landlord, because land stays with its owner, no matter the order of the words.

phrases.english: Even if it is reversed.
phrases.notes: He means that even if the order is flipped, so the deal ends with 'twelve a year,' the landlord still gets the month.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows a case where the two rulings give different results
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן just repeats רב's rule of following the last words.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב נחמן decides by ownership of the land, so the landlord wins even when the wording is reversed.

steps.title: A question to רבי ינאי: Who must prove the rent was paid?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: the renter says he paid, and the landlord says he never received payment. Who has to bring proof?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רבי ינאי: A renter says, 'I paid,' and the landlord says, 'I did not take.' Who has to bring proof?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It brings a question that was asked of רבי ינאי about an argument over whether rent was paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides make opposite claims about one fact: was the rent paid? The question is who carries the burden of proof. Is it the renter, who says he paid, or the landlord, who denies it?

keyTerms.meaning: upon whom is the burden of proof?

phrases.english: They asked of רבי ינאי:
A renter says, 'I gave' [the rent],
and the landlord says, 'I did not take' [it].
Upon whom is it to bring proof?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about rent disputes
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In a dispute over whether rent was paid, which side carries the burden of proof?

steps.title: When was this claim made? Both cases seem already known
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks when the renter made his claim. Whether it was during the rental period or after it, the answer is already known from a משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When? If it was within his time, we already learned it. If it was after his time, we already learned it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the question itself. It points out that both possible cases already seem to be answered. The next step brings the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are only two choices: the claim came during the rental period, or after it ended. For each choice, the גמרא says תנינא, meaning a משנה already covers it. So what were they really asking רבי ינאי?

keyTerms.meaning: within his time (during the rental period)
we already learned it (in a משנה)

phrases.english: When?
phrases.notes: When did the renter say he paid?

phrases.english: If within his time, we already learned it;
if after his time, we already learned it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the question in Step 14
steps.kashyaTarget: The question asked of רבי ינאי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both possible times for the claim are already settled by a משנה, so the question seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The proof: the משנה about redeeming a firstborn
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה about פדיון הבן. Before the 30th day, the son is presumed not redeemed. After it, he is presumed redeemed.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: If the father died within thirty days, the son is presumed not redeemed until he brings proof that he was redeemed. After thirty days, he is presumed redeemed until people tell him that he was not redeemed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its claim from Step 15 that 'we already learned it.' It quotes a משנה about redeeming a firstborn son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A father must redeem his firstborn after 30 days. Before then, we assume he did not pay yet, because people do not pay before they must. After the deadline, we assume he did pay. The same logic answers the rent question both during the rental period and after it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה gives a basic rule: a person does not pay before the payment is due, but he is assumed to pay once it is due. This rule is what makes the question to רבי ינאי look already answered.

phrases.english: As we learned:
If the father died within thirty days
phrases.notes: Thirty days after the birth, when the firstborn must be redeemed.

phrases.english: he is presumed not redeemed
until he brings proof that he was redeemed.
After thirty days,
he is presumed redeemed,
until they tell him that he was not redeemed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the 'תנינא' claims in Step 15
steps.raayaObject: That both times of the rent claim are already settled
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in בכורות about a father who died before or after the 30th day

steps.title: The question is about the last day of the rental
steps.stepSummary: The question is needed for a claim made on the exact day the rental period ends. Do people pay on the due date itself, or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed for a case where the renter makes his claim on the very day his rental period ends. Does a person usually pay on the day the payment is due, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 15. The question is not about the middle of the rental or after it. It is about one exact day: the last day of the rental.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פדיון הבן משנה from step 16 covers 'before the time' and 'after the time.' It does not tell us what happens on the due day itself. So the new question is whether people really pay on the very day payment is due. If they do, the renter is believed. If they usually wait, the landlord is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for this case). Used to show a question or rule still has a real use.
On the day his time is completed, meaning the due date itself
Does a person usually do...? It asks about normal human habits.

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not asking about before or after the due date, because the משנה already covered those. It is only asking about the exact due day.
